question: An intern finishes examining a patient and needs to perform hand hygiene before seeing the next patient. The hands are not visibly soiled and the patient does not have Clostridioides difficile infection. Which hand hygiene method and duration is MOST appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. For routine clinical care with non-soiled hands and no C. difficile exposure, ABHR is the preferred method — it is faster and more effective against transient flora than soap-and-water. The WHO recommends 20–30 seconds to ensure adequate coverage of all hand surfaces.

Incorrect in this context. Soap-and-water handwashing (40–60 seconds) is indicated when hands are visibly soiled or after C. difficile exposure. For routine non-soiled inter-patient hand hygiene, ABHR is preferred because it is faster and provides superior antimicrobial activity against transient flora.

Incorrect. While ABHR is the correct method here, 5–10 seconds is insufficient. The WHO recommends 20–30 seconds to ensure all hand surfaces are adequately covered. Rushed application leaves untreated areas and significantly reduces antimicrobial efficacy.

answers.text: Surgical hand antisepsis with chlorhexidine for 2–5 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Surgical hand antisepsis (2–5 minutes with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine scrub) is reserved for before surgical or invasive procedures. It is excessive and impractical for routine inter-patient hand hygiene on a ward round.

overallFeedback.feedback: For routine inter-patient hand hygiene with non-soiled hands, ABHR for 20–30 seconds is the standard. It is faster and more effective than soap-and-water for removing transient flora. Soap-and-water (40–60 sec) is for soiled hands or C. difficile; surgical scrub (2–5 min) is pre-operative only.

ABHR for 20–30 seconds is the WHO standard for routine clinical hand hygiene. Reserve soap-and-water for visibly soiled hands or C. difficile exposure, and surgical scrub for pre-operative antisepsis.
